title: MYP Language and Literature eAssessment Guide
summary: MYP Language and Literature eAssessment explained: understand the on-screen exam, assessment criteria, grade boundaries and practical preparation.
body_markdown:
The **MYP Language and Literature eAssessment** can feel unfamiliar at first. You are not simply being asked what a text means. You must analyse how meaning is created, organize a convincing response, produce writing for a purpose and use language accurately.


For an MYP Year 5 student, the key fact is reassuring: Language and Literature is assessed through an externally marked **on-screen examination** , not an ePortfolio. The exam uses texts and multimedia material connected by a shared context. Your responses are judged through the four familiar MYP criteria, then converted into a final subject grade from 1 to 7.


This guide follows a student from first understanding the format to preparing for the screen with greater confidence.


### MYP Language and Literature eAssessment at a glance


Before opening a practice task, make sure you understand the basic structure:


- Language and Literature uses an **on-screen examination** in the final year of the MYP.
- The examination lasts **two hours** under the standard published IB format.
- Students work with literary and non-literary material, which may include written, visual and multimedia texts.
- Tasks are linked to one of the MYP global contexts.
- Responses can include analysis, comparison and purposeful writing.
- Work is assessed against four areas: analysing, organizing, producing text and using language.
- The IB awards a final subject grade from **1 to 7** using session-specific grade boundaries.


Schools decide whether to register students for optional MYP eAssessment. Your coordinator should therefore confirm the exact examination session, language and administrative arrangements that apply to you.


### On-screen examination or ePortfolio?


Imagine a Year 5 student hearing the word “eAssessment” for the first time. The word suggests one digital system, but the MYP actually uses different assessment routes for different subject groups.


For **Language and Literature** , the route is an on-screen examination. Students encounter previously unseen material and complete responses under timed conditions. The work is externally marked by IB-appointed examiners.


An **ePortfolio** is different. In subjects assessed through an ePortfolio, classroom work is compiled and submitted electronically before being externally moderated. That is not the standard assessment route for MYP Language and Literature.


This distinction matters because preparation should resemble the real task. Revising only polished coursework will not fully prepare you to interpret unfamiliar material, plan quickly and compose a complete response on screen.


A student asks what a writer is trying to do while a tiny author admits to meeting a deadline


### What the MYP eAssessment format tests


The **MYP eAssessment format** is designed to test transfer rather than memorization. You cannot know the exact source material in advance. What you can learn is a repeatable way to read, think and respond.


A task may ask you to examine choices such as:


- diction, imagery and figurative language
- structure, sequence and narrative perspective
- tone, voice and characterization
- layout, typography, colour or camera choices
- audience, purpose and context
- connections or contrasts between texts


The examination can include several related stimuli rather than one isolated passage. A written extract might sit beside an image or another text, inviting you to compare how each creator presents a shared idea.


Strong answers move beyond identifying a technique. They explain the relationship between **choice, effect and purpose** . “The writer uses repetition” is an observation. “The repetition makes the warning feel unavoidable, reinforcing the speaker’s urgent attempt to influence the audience” is analysis.


### The four MYP Language and Literature criteria


The assessment is built around four criteria. Their wording should already be familiar from classroom learning, although an external examination applies them through specific tasks and mark schemes.


Criterion What it assesses What effective work demonstrates


A: Analysing Interpretation and evaluation of texts Perceptive ideas supported by relevant evidence and analysis of authorial choices


B: Organizing Structure and development A logical line of thought, coherent paragraphs and suitable referencing or presentation conventions


C: Producing text Imaginative or purposeful composition Insight, creativity and deliberate choices suited to the audience, context and purpose


D: Using language Control and appropriateness of language Accurate, varied vocabulary and sentence structures in an effective register and style


### Criterion A: Analysing


Analysis begins with understanding, but it cannot end there. You need to interpret content, recognize important choices and explain their effects. When comparison is required, integrate it into your argument instead of writing two disconnected mini-essays.


Evidence matters. Select short, precise details and explain them fully. A large quotation does not automatically produce a stronger point.


### Criterion B: Organizing


Organization is the architecture beneath the response. Before typing, decide on a central interpretation and the order in which your points will develop it.


Each paragraph should contribute something new. Topic sentences create direction, while transitions show how one idea leads to the next. Clear organization also helps an examiner follow a sophisticated interpretation without having to reconstruct it.


### Criterion C: Producing text


Producing text asks you to write with intention. Depending on the task, you may need to create an imaginative, persuasive or otherwise purposeful piece.


Do not treat the format as a costume. A speech is not just an essay with “Good morning” added at the beginning. Its direct address, rhythm, rhetorical choices and sense of audience should shape the whole response.


### Criterion D: Using language


Language is judged through control and suitability, not through complicated vocabulary alone. Precise words are better than impressive words used incorrectly.


Leave time to check agreement, punctuation, spelling and sentence boundaries. Also check register. Language that suits a personal narrative may be inappropriate in a formal analytical response.


### How MYP grades 1 to 7 are reached


Students sometimes assume that the four classroom criteria can simply be added to produce an examination grade. External eAssessment is more nuanced.


Examiners award marks using the task-specific mark scheme and the relevant assessment criteria. The IB then applies grade boundaries for that examination session to convert the final mark into a subject grade from **1 to 7** , with 7 being the highest.


Grade boundaries should not be treated as permanent percentages. They can be established for a particular session after the IB reviews the demands of the assessment and evidence of candidate performance. This helps preserve comparable standards when one examination is slightly more or less demanding than another.


The practical lesson is simple: do not build your revision around guessing a boundary. Build it around producing complete evidence across all four criteria. A response with excellent ideas can still lose ground through weak organization, an unsuitable format or preventable language errors.


### A practical preparation plan


The student who improves most is not always the one who writes the greatest number of essays. Often, it is the one who studies feedback carefully.


### Practise reading unfamiliar texts


Use short texts, advertisements, speeches, images and extracts. Give yourself a limited period to identify audience, purpose, context and three significant authorial choices. This builds the first skill the examination demands: deciding what matters.


### Plan before writing


A focused three-minute plan can save much more time later. Write a provisional thesis, choose evidence and place your ideas in a logical order. For creative tasks, identify the audience, purpose, register and intended effect before drafting.


### Revise through the criteria


After completing a response, label the evidence for each criterion. Ask:


- Have I interpreted the text rather than summarized it?
- Can a reader follow the development of my argument?
- Does my created text genuinely suit its purpose and audience?
- Is my language controlled, varied and accurate?

### On the day of the MYP Language and Literature exam


Begin by reading the instructions, command terms and source material carefully. A fluent answer to the wrong question remains the wrong answer.


Budget time according to the available marks and the complexity of each task. Keep enough time for proofreading, but do not edit endlessly while a later response remains unfinished. When typing on screen, use clear paragraphs and save or confirm your work as directed by the examination platform and invigilator.


The exam rewards attention more than performance. Read what is actually present. Notice the small choice that changes the tone, the visual detail that shapes the audience’s reaction or the structural shift that complicates the message.


### Meeting the assessment with a clear method


At first, the MYP Language and Literature eAssessment can look like a test of inspiration. It is better understood as a test of disciplined reading and deliberate communication.


You cannot predict every text. You can prepare a method: interpret the task, select evidence, explain choices, organize your thinking and adapt your language to purpose.
